sections.learningObjectives:
- Define fraud, waste, and abuse and distinguish among them based on intent and harm.
- Recognize false-claim, upcoding, unbundling, and kickback concepts and their legal significance.
- Apply documentation-integrity and privacy practices that support accurate, lawful billing.
- Describe the purpose and basic elements of a compliance program, including reporting channels.
- Report suspected fraud, waste, or abuse through the proper channels without fear of retaliation.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Fraud is like cheating on purpose to get money you did not earn — it is a plan to lie for gain, not an accident.

### Question 2

Waste is like leaving all the lights on in an empty house — it costs extra money but nobody is trying to trick anyone.

### Question 3

Fraud means you lied on purpose. Abuse means you did something the wrong way, but maybe without meaning to cheat.

### Question 4

A false claim is like sending a bill for a job you never did — it is asking to be paid for something that is not real.

### Question 5

A kickback is like a secret payment to steer customers your way — it is paying someone to send business, not to do real work.

### Question 6

A compliance program is like the rules and referee in a game — it tells everyone how to play fairly and catches problems early.

### Question 7

If you think a teammate is breaking the rules, you tell the coach (the compliance officer), not a stranger.

### Question 8

Documentation integrity is like keeping an honest diary of your day — write down what really happened, when it happened.

### Question 9

Upcoding is like telling someone you ran a marathon when you only jogged a mile — claiming more than you really did.

### Question 10

Unbundling is like selling a sandwich by charging separately for the bread, the meat, and the cheese instead of one sandwich price.

### Question 11

The Anti-Kickback law is like a rule that says you cannot pay someone a secret fee to send customers to your store.

### Question 12

The Stark Law is like a rule that a referee cannot also own one of the teams and then give that team all the calls.

### Question 13

Waste is like running the dishwasher when it is half empty every single time — money down the drain, but no lie involved.

### Question 14

Abuse is like doing a job in a sloppy, wasteful way that costs extra money — wrong, but maybe not a deliberate cheat.

### Question 15

If you spot a mistake in a school paper before you turn it in, you fix it — you do not pretend it is not there.

### Question 16

The medical record should be a true story of the visit — not a story made up to earn more money.

### Question 17

Whistleblower protection is like a rule that says you cannot punish a teammate for honestly telling the coach something is wrong.

### Question 18

The OIG is like the referee who investigates when someone cheats in a big government program.

### Question 19

A red flag is like a warning light on a car dashboard — billing that does not match the notes tells you something may be wrong.

### Question 20

Medical necessity is like needing medicine when you are sick — the service has to actually be needed for the patient's health.

### Question 21

Write down what happened while it is fresh, like jotting a score right after the game instead of a week later.

### Question 22

A hotline is like a suggestion-and-report box that lets people speak up privately when something seems wrong.

### Question 23

Fraud is like someone stealing from the community piggy bank — everyone pays more and gets less for it.

### Question 24

Writing that you did a chore you never did is a lie on paper — and it can be used to get money for nothing.

### Question 25

Anyone on a team can break the rules — players, coaches, or the whole club — so everyone has to play fair.

### Question 26

If a teammate keeps changing the score to look better, you tell the coach quietly — you do not yell in front of the crowd or secretly erase points.

### Question 27

Paying a doctor a fee for every patient they send over is like bribing someone to send customers — it is against the rules.

### Question 28

If a customer says they were charged for something they never bought, the store investigates instead of insisting the bill is right.

### Question 29

Signing someone else's name on a paper is like forging a note from your parent — it is a lie, no matter who asked.

### Question 30

Fixing a record is like correcting a mistake in a diary with a note that says 'I meant this,' not by tearing out the page.

### Question 31

Saying 'we always write it this way' does not make a made-up note true — a lie is a lie even if everyone does it.

### Question 32

If you find out the team is stealing points in a game, you report it to the referee — you do not help steal more.

### Question 33

Abuse is cutting corners the wrong way without meaning to cheat; fraud is deliberately lying to get money.

### Question 34

Getting paid secretly to push a certain medicine is like taking money to tell people a toy is great just so you get a cut.

### Question 35

Always letting people skip their share of the bill can be a trick to get them to buy more — that is why there are rules about it.

### Question 36

Backdating is like writing yesterday's date on today's homework to make it look on time — it is still a lie.

### Question 37

Copy-pasting the same note every visit is like reusing last week's report card for this week — it does not show what really happened.

### Question 38

Filling in the answer sheet before the test happens is cheating — you cannot write down results that have not happened yet.

### Question 39

Billing is like a receipt — it must match what actually happened, and the medical record is the proof.

### Question 40

Charging two people for the same pizza is double-dipping — you report it, you do not charge a third person.

### Question 41

A compliance program is the set of rules and checkups that help a team follow the law and fix mistakes fast.

### Question 42

When the referee reviews the game, you answer honestly about what happened — you do not change the scorebook.

### Question 43

Filing a false claim is like cheating on your taxes — it can bring big fines and even worse if you meant to do it.

### Question 44

Saying you worked 60 minutes when you worked 20 is padding your timesheet — it is not allowed.

### Question 45

The Stark Law is like a rule that a judge cannot send cases to a court they partly own.

### Question 46

If you hear a plan to hide money that should be returned, you tell the person in charge — quietly, through the right channel.

### Question 47

An overpayment is like a store accidentally giving you too much change — money you were not supposed to keep.

### Question 48

If a store gives you too much change, the right move is to give it back — not to keep it or spend it elsewhere.

### Question 49

The money room — billing and coding — is where cheating is most likely, so that is where the team keeps the closest watch.

### Question 50

Writing down a sickness that was never diagnosed, just to get insurance to pay, is making up a reason on paper.

### Question 51

Qui tam is like a rule that lets a person who knows about cheating help the government catch it — and share the reward.

### Question 52

A free trip for sending business a vendor's way is like a secret bribe — the answer is no, and tell the boss.

### Question 53

The note has to explain why the care was really needed — like showing a doctor's note for missing school.

### Question 54

When you are not sure about a rule, you ask the coach — you do not copy what everyone else is doing.

### Question 55

Monitoring and auditing are like a coach watching practice to fix small mistakes before the big game.

### Question 56

You do not mail bills for work that has no proof, and you do not make up proof — you tell the person in charge.

### Question 57

Anyone on the team can and should report cheating, and the rules say you cannot be punished for telling the truth in good faith.

### Question 58

Helping hide a secret payment is being part of the cheat — the right move is to say no and tell someone in charge.

### Question 59

HIPAA is like a lockbox rule for patient info — the info stays private and correct, and only people who need it may open the box.

### Question 60

Just because you have a key does not mean you may open someone's locker to look around — you use it only for your job.

### Question 61

Minimum necessary is like only opening the one drawer you need at work — not every drawer in the building.

### Question 62

When a teammate leaves the team, you take back their locker key so they cannot get in anymore.

### Question 63

If you want to report quietly, use the official suggestion box — not a public billboard.

### Question 64

Saying a no-show actually came to the office is making up a whole visit — that is cheating, not fixing a missed appointment.

### Question 65

If someone gets paid more every time they send patients a certain way, that is a big warning sign of a kickback.

### Question 66

If a boss tells you to fudge the numbers, the answer is no — and you tell the compliance team, because pressure does not make cheating okay.

### Question 67

An assistant is like a player who follows the rules, keeps honest records, and tells the coach when something looks wrong — not the referee who hands out penalties.

### Question 68

Auto-marking every paper an A+ without reading it is not grading — it is inflating the results.

### Question 69

One rule punishes bribes (you must mean it), while the other is like a 'no owning the team you referee' rule that applies even if you did not mean any harm.

### Question 70

Charging the same thing under several different names, month after month, is a pattern that needs a closer look.

### Question 71

Ordering the same test twice out of habit is like buying two of the same item by mistake — wasteful, not a deliberate cheat.

### Question 72

A good team needs a coach who cares, a rulebook, practice, and a way to speak up — not just one talk on the first day.

### Question 73

If you are handed too much change, you give it back on your own — you do not wait to be caught.

### Question 74

Owning the imaging shop and sending all your patients there is like a referee who also owns one team — the rules step in.

### Question 75

Keeping a second, fake scorebook that says you won is not bookkeeping — it is making up evidence.

### Question 76

Qui tam lets a person who knows about cheating step up for the whole team — and share the prize if the team wins back money.

### Question 77

The safest team keeps honest records, trains everyone, and checks its own work — that is how you avoid cheating and mistakes.

### Question 78

Calling a bribe a 'marketing fee' does not make it okay — paying for referrals is still paying for referrals.

### Question 79

A note written before the visit happened is like a movie review posted before the movie came out — it does not add up.

### Question 80

Fixing a mistake the right way means showing your work — crossing it out and writing the correction, not hiding the eraser marks.

### Question 81

Signing someone else's name on a permission slip is forging their promise — it is a lie that can undo the whole document.

### Question 82

If you realize you have been overcharging, you own it and fix it — you do not hide the receipts.

### Question 83

A real discount lowers the price for the customer; a kickback secretly pays someone to send customers — the difference is the reason behind the money.

### Question 84

If you think you saw cheating but are not 100 percent sure, you still tell the coach — the coach figures out the facts.

### Question 85

A good compliance program is like wearing a seatbelt and driving carefully — it lowers the chance of a crash, but it does not promise you will never be pulled over.
